Coast to Coast: Crossing England on Two Wheels

England's width at its narrowest — from the Irish Sea to the North Sea — is barely 100 miles. But crossing those 100 miles by motorcycle takes you through some of the country's most dramatic landscapes: the Lake District fells, the Pennine spine, and the North York Moors. A coast-to-coast ride is a proper adventure that can be completed in a day or savoured over a long weekend.

The Classic Northern Route (130 miles)

Start at St Bees on the Cumbrian coast and head east over the Lake District passes (Honister, Kirkstone) through the Pennines via Hartside, across the North Pennines to the Durham Dales, and finish at Whitby on the North Sea coast. This route follows approximately the same line as Wainwright's famous Coast to Coast walk but on tarmac.

The Mountain Route (150 miles)

For maximum drama, start at Whitehaven and ride over Hardknott and Wrynose Passes to Ambleside. Cross the Pennines via the A66 to Scotch Corner, then take the A171 through the North York Moors to Whitby. This route packs England's steepest passes and wildest moorland into a single ride.

The Gentle Route (110 miles)

Start at Morecambe and ride through the Forest of Bowland to Settle, then east through the Yorkshire Dales via Wensleydale to Northallerton. Continue east through the Howardian Hills to Scarborough. A less extreme crossing but equally scenic, with gentler gradients and wider roads.

A coast-to-coast ride strips England to its essentials — mountains, moorland, and the sea on both sides. It's the perfect distillation of English riding.

Planning Your Crossing

  • Direction: West to east puts the prevailing wind behind you and the morning sun in front
  • Duration: One long day (10-12 hours) or two relaxed days with an overnight in the Pennines
  • Season: May to September for reliable weather. The passes can be icy from November to March
  • Fuel: Fill up on the coast and in the major towns. Rural Pennine areas have limited fuel

Making It a Weekend

The best coast-to-coast weekend starts with a Friday evening ride to Keswick or Penrith. Saturday, ride west to the coast, then back across England to Whitby. Sunday, explore the North York Moors and return home. Alternatively, ride east on Saturday and return via a different route on Sunday — the variety of crossings means no two coast-to-coast rides need be the same.

What to Expect

The west coast is wetter than the east — expect rain in the Lake District even on days that start sunny. The Pennine crossing is exposed to wind and can be cold even in summer. The east coast finish at Whitby rewards you with fish and chips, 199 steps to the abbey, and a well-earned pint overlooking the harbour. It's a fitting end to any crossing. keyTakeaways: England's narrowest width, Irish Sea to North Sea, is barely 100 miles but crosses the Lakes, Pennines and North York Moors.
The Classic Northern Route (130 miles) runs St Bees to Whitby, echoing Wainwright's Coast to Coast walk.
The Mountain Route (150 miles) from Whitehaven adds Hardknott and Wrynose for maximum drama.
The Gentle Route (110 miles) from Morecambe uses the Forest of Bowland and Dales for easier gradients.
Ride west to east to put the prevailing wind behind you; expect the west coast to be wetter.

faq.q: How long does a coast-to-coast ride take?
faq.a: It can be done in one long day of 10 to 12 hours, or savoured over two relaxed days with an overnight in the Pennines. The narrowest crossing is barely 100 miles as the crow flies, but the mountain and moorland detours push the riding distance to between 110 and 150 miles depending on the route you choose.

West to east is the classic choice. It puts the prevailing wind behind you and the morning sun in front, and it builds towards a satisfying seaside finish. Expect the west coast to be noticeably wetter than the east, so it can be raining in the Lake District even on a day that starts sunny at your destination.

faq.q: What is the most dramatic version?
faq.a: The Mountain Route at 150 miles. Start at Whitehaven, ride over Hardknott and Wrynose Passes to Ambleside, cross the Pennines via the A66 to Scotch Corner, then take the A171 through the North York Moors to Whitby. This packs England's steepest passes and wildest moorland into a single ride, but demands respect in poor conditions.

faq.q: When is the best season to cross?
faq.a: May to September gives the most reliable weather. The high passes such as Hardknott, Wrynose and Honister can be icy from November to March and occasionally close, so avoid winter unless conditions are settled. The Pennine crossing is exposed to wind and can feel cold even in summer, so pack layers whatever the forecast.

Fill up on the coast and in the major towns before heading inland, because rural Pennine areas have limited fuel. The gentler crossings pass through Settle and Northallerton with easy fuel, while the mountain routes run through remote country. Finish at Whitby with fish and chips, the 199 steps to the abbey and a well-earned pint by the harbour.
